newsitem.title: RUSSIA: GM plans joint drive into Russian wilds.
newsitem.headline: GM plans joint drive into Russian wilds.

text.p: General Motors Corp. took its second leap into Russian car production Wednesday when it announced plans to build a new car in the country by the end of 1998 together with Finnish and Russian partners.

In the first such project between major Russian and foreign car makers, GM subsidiary Adam Opel, Finland's Valmet Oy Automotive and dominant Russian car maker AvtoVAZ will build a 30,000-50,000 car assembly plant in north-west Russia.
Later, production of the new Opel model will also take place deep in Russia at AvtoVAZ's Togliatti plant, which produces Lada cars, they said.
Russia's AVVA, which works with AvtoVAZ, is also a partner in the $62 million plant, which Valmet will manage on a daily basis, the partners said.
"We provide a car and the technical details that go with it and they start coming back with substituted content," Opel Chairman David Herman told Reuters.
The new plant will simply assemble vehicles from imported parts with a long-term view to finding local suppliers and bringing in foreign ones.

Valmet President Juhani Riutta told Reuters he expected to get customs and tax breaks on the cars but that if partial local production did not begin within a few years, the breaks would probably vanish. "They are not for free," he said.
Valmet already works with both GM and AvtoVAZ.
The partners said they hoped to announce a ground-breaking date in mid-summer for the plant, on a site yet to be determined.
They have agreed on a business plan but have not signed a final agreement and declined to give forecasts of the cost or time frame for later stages of the plan.
Russian and foreign car makers have been eyeing each other for years, but had not been able to come to an agreement.
GM inaugurated a plant assembling its Chevrolet Blazers in the Russian Tatarstan Republic last December but the U.S. automaker itself controls the plant.

AvtoVAZ, which produces almost 80 percent of Russian cars, has severe financial problems. It owes hundreds of millions of dollars in back taxes and the government is forcing it to hand over half its shares to guarantee back payments.

Valmet's Riutta told reporters his company made the relationship possible. "There is a natural ambition by the Russian side to be in control and a natural ambition by Opel, so the tip of the scale is given to Valmet."
A sharp slide in Russian auto production after the breakup of the Soviet Union has reversed and Russian output increased 4 percent last year though quality is still lacking.

AVVA Chief Executive Nikolai Kosov told a news conference the new plant would be financed by contributions from Opel and Valmet, sales of discounted sovereign debt owed by Russia to Finland and loans from international and Finnish financial institutions.
Kosov told reporters Russian and Finnish Prime Ministers Viktor Chernomyrdin and Paavo Lipponen had seen the new Opel to be built in Russia, which he said is not currently sold.
"It is clear that this car is of the next class up from ours, so it is not a competitor," AvtoVAZ Chairman Vladimir Kadannikov told the news conference.
Chernomyrdin will open a new assembly plant by South Korea's KIA Motors in Western Russian Kaliningrad on Friday, but no major Russian automakers are in that venture.

AvtoVAZ has looked for a foreign partner to take a large piece of its own equity and has mentioned Opel as a possible suitor, though a GM official said the company had no plans to take a stake in AvtoVAZ itself.
GM's stock was unchanged at $56.75 on the New York Stock Exchange in afternoon trading.
